This is the fourth time that this has been posted in the past couple days. What most of you all don't realize is that the cross section of a steel member is only relevant to knowing the exact load capacity of that section. The more important thing to understand is the stress (force/area) behavior of the material when heated. In the case of structural steel, when heated to 1000F, the material losses 40-50% of its allowable stress capacity. That means for the same cross section, the allowable load that section can support is reduced to half of what it was. This is what the guy in the video understands and is illustrating to you all. After all, how the else do you think that we can even fabricate steel beams? The principals at work are the same.

Typical structure and house fires can easily reach 1000F, which is why we've seen other steel frame buildings fail without having planes rammed into them or controlled demolitions. For those who want to split hairs over partial vs total collapse, you're wrong and just moving the goal posts. The mechanisms at play are identical and buildings are complex systems composed of countless variables which must be controlled for when analyzing a structure. In other words, there is no telling how a building will behave without exhaustive analysis which investigates all variables in a scenario.

The reason so few steel frame (and subsequently other modern buildings) have collapses is because of the development of building design codes and adherence to them in the modern era. Fire prevention measures are tested to death in order to prevent just such incidents from occurring, but no one can account for everything in a design or it would be cost prohibitive and take forever to design.
